y-m-17-01.title: How long should I draw the 3 km on the map?
y-m-17-01.topic: Scale: the ratio of length on the map to real length
y-m-17-01.goal: Work out which way the scale links the length on the map and the real length to find the mistake in a solution, and make several (length on the map, scale) pairs that fit the same real length.
y-m-17-01.material: You want to draw the walking trail in front of the school on a map. At the bottom of the map, the scale '1 : 50000' (one to fifty thousand) is written. This means 1 cm on the map is 50000 cm in real life, and the whole map is shrunk by the same ratio. 1 km is 100000 cm. Mina solved 'How many cm should I draw on the map for a trail that is really 3 km?' as below.
y-m-17-01.thinking.0: Finding the line that goes wrong in a solution
y-m-17-01.thinking.1: Choosing ways to check whether a result makes sense
y-m-17-01.thinking.2: Making several cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-17-01.prereq.0: Knowing that the scale (e.g. 1 : 50000) is the ratio of the length on the map to the real length
y-m-17-01.prereq.1: Relations between units of length (1 km = 100000 cm)
y-m-17-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Mina's solution.
y-m-17-01.s.s1.hint.0: Look at the result first. Is it okay for the length to draw on the map to become much longer than the real length of 300000 cm?
y-m-17-01.s.s1.hint.1: Using ‘1 cm on the map is 50000 cm in real life’ from line 2 just as it is, write in order how many real cm 2 cm and 3 cm on the map would be.
y-m-17-01.s.s1.line.1: 1 cm on the map is 50000 cm in real life, so (length on the map) = (real length) × 50000.
y-m-17-01.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the trail should be drawn on the map as 15000000000 cm.
y-m-17-01.s.s1.explain: The mistake starts at line 2. The scale 1 : 50000 means the real length is 50000 times the length on the map, so to find the length on the map you have to divide the real length by 50000, not multiply by 50000. The calculation in line 3 follows line 2 so the calculation itself is right but the result is strange, and line 4 is wrong for the same reason. Worked out correctly, it is drawn as 6 cm on the map.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.prompt: Which checks help you notice that Mina's result is strange? Choose all the suitable ones.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.hint.0: For each choice, compare ‘would this check let you tell that the thinking is wrong, or does it just repeat the same thinking?’
y-m-17-01.s.s2.hint.1: Change the 15000000000 cm that Mina found into km, and think about whether it is a length that can be drawn on one map.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.o.a: Press the same calculation on a calculator once more to see whether the same value as the first comes out
y-m-17-01.s.s2.r.a: If you calculate with the same thinking, the same value comes out again. Whether the calculation is right and whether the thinking (the equation) is right are different matters.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.o.b: The number is too big, so just writing the unit in km makes it the right value
y-m-17-01.s.s2.r.b: If you only change the unit, the number you write changes but the length stays the same. 15000000000 cm is 150000 km, which is far too long to draw on a map.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.o.c: Write in order how many real cm 1 cm, 2 cm, and 3 cm on the map are
y-m-17-01.s.s2.r.c: If you spell out the meaning of the scale in a sentence, you can see which direction is bigger.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.o.d: Use common sense to ask whether the length drawn on the map can be longer than the real length
y-m-17-01.s.s2.r.d: You are checking whether the result makes sense with the basic idea that a map is a shrunken drawing of the real thing.
y-m-17-01.s.s2.explain: If you spell out the meaning of the scale like 1 cm → 50000 cm and 2 cm → 100000 cm, or look at the result with the common sense that a map must be smaller than reality, you can tell that the direction of multiplying is off. Doing the same calculation again may repeat the same mistake.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.prompt: This time, thinking correctly, you want to draw a road that is really 2 km as a cm on the map (a natural number from 4 to 20). Make two scales '1 : b' you could use, with two different lengths on the map.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.hint.0: First choose a, and think about how many real cm 1 cm on the map must be for a cm to add up to 200000 cm. That value is b.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.hint.1: After choosing a and b, check backwards whether a cm on the map becomes 200000 cm in reality, and try once more with a different a.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.var.a: Length of 2 km on the map (cm)
y-m-17-01.s.s3.var.b: In the scale 1 : □, the □ (a natural number)
y-m-17-01.s.s3.ok.c1: The length on the map is a natural number from 4 cm to 20 cm.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.fail.c1: The length on the map a must be a natural number from 4 to 20.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.ok.c2: The □ of the scale is a natural number.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.fail.c2: The □ (b) of the scale must be a natural number.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.ok.c3: a cm on the map stands for a real 2 km (200000 cm).
y-m-17-01.s.s3.fail.c3: a cm on the map does not become 200000 cm in reality. Check again how many real cm 1 cm on the map is.
y-m-17-01.s.s3.explain: e.g. For 4 cm it is 1 : 50000, for 5 cm it is 1 : 40000, for 8 cm it is 1 : 25000, and for 10 cm it is 1 : 20000. Even for the same 2 km, the longer you draw it on the map, the smaller the □ of the scale needs to be (a more detailed map).

y-m-17-02.title: If you use two coupons, is it the same as a 30% discount?
y-m-17-02.topic: Percentages: applying discount rates one after another
y-m-17-02.goal: Test the first idea of adding discount rates with numerical examples, revise your judgment and confidence each time new information comes out, and explain what standard a percentage refers to.
y-m-17-02.material: An online shop has two coupons. Coupon 가 is '20% off the regular price', and Coupon 나 is 'another 10% off the discounted price', and you can use both 가 and 나 one after the other. Minseo said, “20% and 10% make 30% together, so it's the same as a 30% discount!” All regular prices are natural numbers (in 원) greater than 0원, and we use only prices that divide out exactly in 원.
y-m-17-02.thinking.0: Forming a first judgment and revising it with evidence
y-m-17-02.thinking.1: Finding the base quantity of a percentage
y-m-17-02.thinking.2: Sorting what one example tells from what it cannot tell
y-m-17-02.prereq.0: Meaning of a percentage (the rate when the base quantity is 100)
y-m-17-02.prereq.1: Finding a discounted price from the regular price and the discount rate
y-m-17-02.s.s1.prompt: Check whether Minseo's statement is right by choosing your own thinking each time new information comes out.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, separate ‘what you can say with only the information known now’ from ‘what you don't know yet.’
y-m-17-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the thinking you chose in the earlier step fits the new information, and say whether your confidence grew or shrank.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.info: The regular price has not been told yet. There is only Minseo's statement and the coupon rules.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Choose the one closest to what you think now.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.after: There is no evidence yet, so any thought is fine as a first guess. Now let's put in a number and test it.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: They seem to be the same. Because 20% and 10% make 30%
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is the idea of adding the discount rates together. You haven't yet asked what the second 10% is 10% of.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: They seem to be different. Because the second 10% applies to a value that is not the original price
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You noticed that the base of the second discount changes.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I can't judge because I don't know the regular price. I want to put in a number and calculate
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You admitted what you don't know and first found a way to test.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.info: I calculated with sneakers whose regular price is 10000원. With Coupon 가, a 20% discount makes 8000원, and then with Coupon 나, a 10% discount makes 7200원. A single 30% discount makes 7000원.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: What can you say from this one calculation?
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.after: If the values differ at 10000원, the claim that 'they are always the same' is already broken. But you need to look more at what happens with other regular prices and how the difference changes.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: When the regular price is 10000원, the values are different, so Minseo's statement does not hold in this case
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You noticed that one example can break 'always the same.'
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 7200원 is close to 7000원, so Minseo's statement is mostly right
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 'The same' and 'similar' are different. You have to consider how to view the 200원 difference.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is different only at this regular price and might be the same at other regular prices, so I need to test more
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a careful attitude of not speaking about all regular prices from one regular price.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.info: I changed the regular price and calculated. 5000원: 4000원 → 3600원, and a single 30% discount gives 3500원. 20000원: 16000원 → 14400원, and a single 30% discount gives 14000원. 100원: 80원 → 72원, and a single 30% discount gives 70원.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: As the regular price changes, how do the values of the two methods compare?
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.after: For all three regular prices, the two-coupon price is 72% of the regular price and the 30%-discount price is 70% of the regular price. Whether there is a regular price where they are the same needs more checking, but so far the evidence points to them always being different.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The bigger the regular price, the closer the two values become
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: At 20000원 the difference became 400원, which actually got bigger. Check yourself whether the difference gets smaller.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Even when the regular price changes, the price after using two coupons is a little more expensive than the 30% discount price
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You read the repeating pattern that the same side is more expensive for all three regular prices.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Depending on the regular price, there may be a regular price where they are the same
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The same side was more expensive all three times. Whether there is a regular price where they are the same can be known only by changing the regular price more or by setting up an equation.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.info: This time I changed the coupon order and used the 10% coupon first and the 20% coupon second. Regular price 10000원: 9000원 → 7200원.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.ask: What can you say about the order of the coupons?
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.after: Even when the order was changed, it was the same, 7200원. You can explain that applying 90% to 80% of the regular price gives the same result as applying 80% to 90%.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.o.a: You should use the bigger discount first to get a lower price
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.r.a: Both orders give 7200원. In this calculation there is no difference depending on the order.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.o.b: At this regular price the values of the two orders are the same. We need to check more whether it is also so for other regular prices
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You spoke carefully without generalizing from one result.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.o.c: I think the value is the same even if the order is changed. Because only the order of multiplying the price by 0.8 and 0.9 is different
y-m-17-02.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You explained by looking at the structure in which the order of the multipliers changes.
y-m-17-02.s.s1.reflect: If you first chose 'the same,' write how the calculation with the regular price 10000원 changed your judgment; if you chose 'different' or 'not sure,' write how that judgment became firmer. Also compare how your degree of confidence differed when there was one example and when there were three.
y-m-17-02.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to send to Minseo. Taking a regular price in 원 as an example, compare the price after using the two coupons in turn with the 30%-discount price and tell Minseo whether the statement is right.
y-m-17-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a regular price that is easy to calculate with, and first find the value after applying the two coupons in turn.
y-m-17-02.s.s2.hint.1: For the same regular price, find the value when 30% is taken off at once, and place the two values side by side to compare.
y-m-17-02.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. If the regular price is ...원, ...
y-m-17-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: For the regular price you gave, did you do both calculations (two coupons / 30% discount)?
y-m-17-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say what the second 10% is 10% of?
y-m-17-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you think once more about whether the conclusion is the same when the regular price changes?
y-m-17-02.s.s2.model.0: No. If the regular price is 10000원, 20% off makes 8000원, and taking another 10% off that makes 7200원. Taking 30% off at once makes 7000원, so the values are different.
y-m-17-02.s.s2.model.1: The second 10% is 10% of the already discounted price, not of the regular price. If the regular price is 5000원, only 400원, 10% of 4000원, is taken off, making 3600원, which is 100원 more than the 30% discount price of 3500원.
y-m-17-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer checked the same way even when the regular price is different.

y-m-17-03.title: Can we know the fourth day from the numbers of sign-ups on three days alone?
y-m-17-03.topic: Rules and correspondence: can a table alone fix the rule?
y-m-17-03.goal: Know that there may be more than one rule that fits the first few values of a table, and say what more information is needed to fix just one.
y-m-17-03.material:
On the reading club's website, 2 people joined on the first day, 4 on the second day, and 8 on the third day. The same person does not join twice, and the number who join on the fourth day is not known yet.
Day | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
New members that day (people) | 2 | 4 | 8 | ?
Jihu said, “The fourth day is 16 people!” and Bora said, “No, I think it will be 14 people.”
y-m-17-03.thinking.0: Sorting out the rules that fit the table
y-m-17-03.thinking.1: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-17-03.thinking.2: Saying what additional information is needed
y-m-17-03.prereq.0: Finding a rule by looking at how two quantities change in a table
y-m-17-03.prereq.1: Saying how numbers grow (by how much they increase, how many times they become)
y-m-17-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the rules that fit all three values in the table (2, 4, 8).
y-m-17-03.s.s1.hint.0: With each rule, make the values for the first, second, and third days in order and compare them with the values in the table.
y-m-17-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write the ‘amount of increase’ separately (from 2 to 4, from 4 to 8) and check whether it matches the statement in the choice.
y-m-17-03.s.s1.o.a: The number of new members on a day is 2 times the number the day before
y-m-17-03.s.s1.r.a: From the first day to the third day, 2, 4, 8 follow in order. You read it as the rule of 2 times.
y-m-17-03.s.s1.o.b: A rule where the number keeps growing by exactly 2 people every day
y-m-17-03.s.s1.r.b: Looking only at the first and second days, it grew by 2 people, but from the second day to the third day it grew by 4 people. Check all three values.
y-m-17-03.s.s1.o.c: The amount of increase gets bigger: 2 people, 4 people, 6 people…
y-m-17-03.s.s1.r.c: This reading looks at how the amount of increase itself changes. It matches that from 2 to 4 it grew by 2 and from 4 to 8 it grew by 4.
y-m-17-03.s.s1.o.d: The number of new members on a day is the day number multiplied by 2
y-m-17-03.s.s1.r.d: It is right for the first day, 2, and the second day, 4, but check what the third day would be.
y-m-17-03.s.s1.explain: The rule of 2 times (2, 4, 8, 16…) and the rule where the amount of increase grows by 2 each time (2, 4, 8, 14…) have the same first three values. The rule of growing by 2 people each day or the rule of multiplying the day number by 2 does not fit the value for the third day.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.prompt: What is the most suitable thought about what Jihu and Bora said?
y-m-17-03.s.s2.hint.0: Make the first to third days with Jihu's rule and Bora's rule and check whether each matches the table.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.hint.1: When two rules fit the table, think about whether the value for the fourth day could tell you which rule it is.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.o.a: Looking at the table, Jihu's 16 people is surely right and Bora is wrong
y-m-17-03.s.s2.r.a: It is true that the rule of 2 times fits, but you need to question whether only one rule fits the table.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.o.b: Looking at the table, Bora's 14 people is surely right and Jihu is wrong
y-m-17-03.s.s2.r.b: Bora's rule also fits the table, but you did not check whether another rule is possible.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.o.c: The two people's rules do not fit the values in the table, so both are wrong
y-m-17-03.s.s2.r.c: The values the two people gave each came from a rule that fits the table. Make the rules again and check.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.o.d: Both are rules that fit the table, so it can't be fixed from the table alone
y-m-17-03.s.s2.r.d: You confirmed that two rules fit the table and held off on judging.
y-m-17-03.s.s2.explain: With the rule of 2 times it is 16 people, and if the amount of increase grows by 2 each time it is 14 people. The three values in the table fit both rules, so three values alone cannot fix the fourth day as one value.
y-m-17-03.s.s3.prompt: What more would you need to know to fix the number of sign-ups on the fourth day as one value? Write the information you need to know, and also write how that information would tell which of the two rules it is.
y-m-17-03.s.s3.hint.0: Try to see whether knowing the value for the fourth day lets you tell which of the two rules is right.
y-m-17-03.s.s3.hint.1: Think about which rule would be natural if you knew how sign-ups actually happen (who brings whom).
y-m-17-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If I had the information I wrote, would it really be settled as one of the two rules?
y-m-17-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about why or how the sign-ups grow?
y-m-17-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think that there may be more than two rules that fit the table?
y-m-17-03.s.s3.model.0: If we know how many people actually joined on the fourth day, we can tell right away whether it is 16 or 14. Also, if the way people join is fixed, such as each friend bringing one friend, we can tell whether it is the rule of 2 times.
y-m-17-03.s.s3.model.1: It would be good to know the fifth day's sign-ups too. If it is 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 it doubles each time, and if it is 2, 4, 8, 14, 22 it is the rule where the amount of increase grows by 2 each time.
y-m-17-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Looking at one more next value.

y-m-17-04.title: To split marbles in the ratio 3 : 2, what must the total number be like?
y-m-17-04.topic: Proportional distribution: dividing by a ratio and conditions on the total
y-m-17-04.goal: Test the claim 'if the total is odd, it can't be split 3 : 2' with a counterexample, and find the condition on the total number for which it can be split by the ratio.
y-m-17-04.material: You want to put marbles into Box 가 and Box 나. The ratio of the numbers of marbles in the two boxes is to be 3 : 2 (three to two), marbles cannot be split into pieces, and both boxes get at least 1 marble. Yuri said, “If the total number of marbles is odd, you can't split it 3 : 2. An odd number can't be split equally!”
y-m-17-04.thinking.0: Testing a general claim with a counterexample
y-m-17-04.thinking.1: Making your own examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-17-04.thinking.2: Stating the condition under which it holds
y-m-17-04.prereq.0: Meaning of the ratio 3 : 2 (if one side is 3 groups, the other side is 2 groups)
y-m-17-04.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable way to check whether Yuri's claim is right?
y-m-17-04.s.s1.hint.0: First look at whether Yuri's statement says 'always' or says 'in some cases.'
y-m-17-04.s.s1.hint.1: Start with 3 in one box and decide the other box while keeping the ratio. Check whether the total is odd or even.
y-m-17-04.s.s1.o.a: An odd number can't be split equally, so say right away that it is right
y-m-17-04.s.s1.r.a: 3 : 2 is not splitting equally. Tell apart 'splitting equally' and 'splitting by a ratio.'
y-m-17-04.s.s1.o.b: Look for one case in which the total is odd and it splits 3 : 2
y-m-17-04.s.s1.r.b: The statement 'it never works' is broken by one case that works. You are trying to find such an example.
y-m-17-04.s.s1.o.c: Try splitting 7 odd marbles 3 : 2, and if it doesn't work, say Yuri is right
y-m-17-04.s.s1.r.c: Just because 7 doesn't work doesn't mean other odd numbers don't work. One failed case cannot speak for 'all odd numbers.'
y-m-17-04.s.s1.o.d: Say you can't test because you don't know the number of marbles
y-m-17-04.s.s1.r.d: You can fix a number of marbles and test it. You just need to try several numbers.
y-m-17-04.s.s1.explain: The claim 'no odd number works' is broken by finding just one odd number that splits 3 : 2. Finding many odd numbers that don't work, like 7, does not confirm that the claim is right.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.prompt: Make two different examples that show Yuri's claim is wrong. The total is an odd number of marbles, 가 : 나 = 3 : 2, and the total is 100 or fewer.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.hint.0: Try 3 marbles in Box 가 and 2 in Box 나. Also find other numbers for which the ratio is 3 : 2, and compare whether the total is odd or even.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the total is odd or even when one group is 1 marble and when it is 2 marbles, and pick a group size that gives an odd total.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.ok.c1: Both boxes have a natural number of marbles.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Marbles cannot be split, and both boxes must have at least 1.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The ratio of the numbers is not 3 : 2. Check whether, when 가 is 3 groups, 나 is 2 groups.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The total is an odd number of marbles.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The total is an even number of marbles. It has to be an example where the total is odd.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.explain: e.g. (3, 2) has a total of 5, (9, 6) has a total of 15, and (15, 10) has a total of 25, all odd. If one group is 1, 3, or 5 marbles, the total grows to 5, 15, 25…. If one group is an even number of marbles (2, 4…), the total is even.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.prompt: What will you say to Yuri? Explain using the examples you made, and write one case, if there is one, where it is odd and still cannot be split 3 : 2.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: You may take the numbers from your two examples as they are. First write the numbers in the two boxes, then check the total.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write in one sentence which part of Yuri's statement is wrong.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. No, if there are ... marbles, then ...
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is there really an example that is odd and 3 : 2?
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: If there is an example of an odd number that cannot be split, did you say why it can't?
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you know and write that 'one example is enough'?
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.model.0: No. If there are 15 marbles, putting 9 in Box 가 and 6 in Box 나 gives 9 : 6 = 3 : 2, and 15 is odd. An odd number that is not a multiple of 5, like 7, can't be split 3 : 2.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.model.1: Even though it is odd, 5 can be split into 3 and 2, so Yuri's statement is wrong. The total just has to be a multiple of 5, like 5, 15, 25.
y-m-17-04.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: I left out an example of an odd number that doesn't work, but the counterexamples are enough.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.prompt: For what total number of marbles can they be split 3 : 2? Choose all the numbers that can be split. (Marbles cannot be split into pieces, and both boxes get at least 1.)
y-m-17-04.s.s3.hint.0: For each choice, check whether the total can be divided equally into as many groups as the sum of the ratio.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.hint.1: For the numbers you think can be split, actually write the numbers for 가 and 나 and check whether the ratio is 3 : 2.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.r.a: See whether you split the 35 marbles into two boxes and checked the ratio.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.r.b: 42 is even, but it doesn't work just because it is even. Split it 3 : 2 and check whether the number in each box is a natural number.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.r.c: See whether you split the 40 marbles into two boxes and checked the ratio.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.r.d: Split 48 marbles 3 : 2 and check whether one box comes out as a natural number.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.r.e: See whether you split the 45 marbles into two boxes and checked the ratio.
y-m-17-04.s.s3.explain: 3 : 2 means dividing the total into 5 groups and giving 3 groups to one side and 2 groups to the other, so the total just has to be a multiple of 5. 35 can be split into 21 and 14, 40 into 24 and 16, and 45 into 27 and 18. 42 and 48 cannot be divided equally into 5 groups.

y-m-17-05.title: If both grow together, is it direct proportion?
y-m-17-05.topic: The conditions that separate direct proportion from inverse proportion
y-m-17-05.goal: Using the values in a table, work out whether two quantities are in direct proportion, tell apart 'both grow' from 'grow by the same number of times,' and explain what assumption is needed when the quantities change in opposite ways.
y-m-17-05.material:
Look at the tables for five situations and see whether the two quantities are in direct proportion. Direct proportion is the relation in which, when one quantity becomes 2 times or 3 times, the other quantity also becomes 2 times or 3 times in the same way.
(가) Number of apples and price: 1 apple 800원, 2 apples 1600원, 3 apples 2400원 (every apple costs the same)
(나) Distance by taxi and fare: 1 km 3500원, 2 km 4000원, 4 km 5000원 (base fare 3000원 plus 500원 for every 1 km)
(다) Time walked and distance walked: 10 minutes 800 m, 20 minutes 1600 m, 30 minutes 2400 m (walking without rest at the same speed)
(라) Number of people working and days to finish the job: 2 people 12 days, 4 people 6 days, 6 people 4 days (everyone works at the same speed and they don't get in each other's way)
(마) Age and height: age 6 115 cm, age 9 133 cm, age 12 150 cm
y-m-17-05.thinking.0: Judging a relation from the evidence in a table
y-m-17-05.thinking.1: Telling apart relations that look similar
y-m-17-05.thinking.2: Stating the conditions under which a relation holds
y-m-17-05.prereq.0: Meaning of direct proportion (when one becomes 2 times or 3 times, the other also becomes 2 times or 3 times)
y-m-17-05.prereq.1: Reading how two quantities change together in a table
y-m-17-05.s.s1.prompt: From the values in the tables, choose all the situations in which the two quantities are in direct proportion.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.hint.0: Pick two rows in the table where one value becomes 2 times or 3 times, calculate how many times the other value becomes, and compare.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.hint.1: Even though the values in (나) and (마) grow together, judge whether they are in direct proportion by whether they become the same number of times.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.r.a: Look at how many times the fare becomes when the distance doubles from 1 km to 2 km.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.r.b: This is the thinking of checking in the table that when the number is 2 times or 3 times, the price also becomes the same number of times.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.r.c: Look at how many times the height becomes when the age doubles from 6 to 12.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.r.d: This is the thinking of checking in the table that when the time is 2 times or 3 times, the distance also becomes the same number of times.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.o.e: (라) Number of people working and number of days
y-m-17-05.s.s1.r.e: Look at how the number of days changes when the number of people doubles. Check whether they grow together.
y-m-17-05.s.s1.explain: In (가) and (다), when one is 2 times or 3 times, the other is also 2 times or 3 times. In (나), when the distance doubles from 1 km to 2 km, the fare goes from 3500원 to 4000원 and does not double, and in (마), even when the age doubles from 6 to 12, the height does not double. In (라), as the number of people grows the number of days falls, so it is not direct proportion.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.prompt: In (나), the taxi fare also increases as the distance increases, but we don't call it direct proportion. What is the most suitable reason?
y-m-17-05.s.s2.hint.0: Recall that the apples in (가) also increase in price by a steady amount, and compare whether increasing steadily tells (나) and (가) apart.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.hint.1: In (나), compare the fare at 1 km and the fare at 2 km and find how many times it became.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.o.a: The fare also grows as the distance grows, so we can't call it direct proportion
y-m-17-05.s.s2.r.a: Growing together is also true of direct proportion. In (가) too, the price grows as the number of apples grows.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.o.b: The fare increases by a steady amount each time the distance increases, so we can't call it direct proportion
y-m-17-05.s.s2.r.b: In (가) too, the price increases steadily by 800원 each time one more apple is added. Increasing steadily alone does not tell them apart.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.o.c: Even when the distance becomes 2 times or 4 times, the fare does not become the same number of times
y-m-17-05.s.s2.r.c: You read the table in light of defining direct proportion as a relation that changes by the same number of times.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.o.d: A taxi fare has a base fare, so it is hard to read the table
y-m-17-05.s.s2.r.d: Being hard to read is not a reason it isn't direct proportion. You have to judge by how the values change.
y-m-17-05.s.s2.explain: Direct proportion is not 'grows together' but 'grows by the same number of times.' Even though the fare increases steadily by 500원, because of the base fare of 3000원, the fare does not double when the distance doubles.
y-m-17-05.s.s3.prompt: In (라), what happens to the number of days when the number of people becomes 2 times or 3 times? Write how it differs from (다), and also write at least one assumption about the people working that is needed for the table's values to be this way.
y-m-17-05.s.s3.hint.0: Read the number of days when the number of people is 2 times and 3 times from the table, and compare it side by side with the table for (다).
y-m-17-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what situations could make the values in the table go off when more people work.
y-m-17-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. When the number of people doubles, ...
y-m-17-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use the values in the table (2 people 12 days, 4 people 6 days) as an example?
y-m-17-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Unlike (다), did you say that when one gets bigger the other gets smaller?
y-m-17-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about cases in real life where this table could go off?
y-m-17-05.s.s3.model.0: When the number of people becomes 2 times or 3 times, the number of days drops from 12 days to 6 days and 4 days, to a half and a third. When one gets bigger, the other gets smaller, the opposite of (다). This happens only if everyone works at the same speed and they don't get in each other's way.
y-m-17-05.s.s3.model.1: If 2 people take 12 days, 4 people take 6 days. The more people there are, the fewer days it takes, so it is not direct proportion; it changes the opposite way. We have to assume that everyone works without rest and does the same amount.
y-m-17-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that gave the values in the table as evidence.

y-m-17-06.title: Which classroom is less crowded? A classroom we decide
y-m-17-06.topic: Comparing by rate: how crowded something is, like population density
y-m-17-06.goal: Know that two different standards for comparing how crowded rooms are can both be used, do not get the direction wrong (whether a bigger value means more crowded or less crowded), and make several classrooms that fit the conditions.
y-m-17-06.material: You want to compare how crowded classrooms are. Think of every classroom as having no furniture, with the whole floor used by students. Room 가 has 24 students and a floor of 36 m² (square meters). Doyun compared it with Room 나 (30 students, floor 40 m²) and solved as below.
y-m-17-06.thinking.0: Choosing a standard for comparison and judging the direction
y-m-17-06.thinking.1: Finding an error in a solution
y-m-17-06.thinking.2: Making several cases that satisfy the constraints
y-m-17-06.prereq.0: Expressing the ratio of two quantities as how much per one of a quantity (a rate)
y-m-17-06.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of decimals and fractions
y-m-17-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the things that can be used as a way to compare how crowded classrooms are.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think of a way to compare which is bigger if you could make Room 가 and Room 나 have the same number of students.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, write separately ‘did it use both the number of students and the area?’ and ‘when the value is bigger, which one is more crowded?’
y-m-17-06.s.s1.o.a: Compare the floor area per student. The smaller it is, the more crowded
y-m-17-06.s.s1.r.a: You used the area per person as the standard for comparison. You also need to write the direction that a smaller value means more crowded.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.o.b: Compare only the number of students. The room with more students is more crowded
y-m-17-06.s.s1.r.b: A big room can be roomy even with many students. You did not look at the floor area together.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.o.c: Compare the value of the number of students minus the floor area and pick the room with the bigger value
y-m-17-06.s.s1.r.c: Subtracting quantities with different units, like people and m², has no meaning. For Room 가, 24 − 36 = −12, and we can't tell what that means.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.o.d: Compare only the floor area of the classrooms. The room with the bigger floor is less crowded
y-m-17-06.s.s1.r.d: If there are a great many students, even a big room can be crowded. You did not look at the number of students together.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.o.e: Compare how many students there are per 1 m² of floor. The bigger it is, the more crowded
y-m-17-06.s.s1.r.e: This is the opposite standard of comparison, turning the number of students into area. The direction that a bigger value means more crowded is opposite to the area per person.
y-m-17-06.s.s1.explain: Area per person (smaller means more crowded) and students per 1 m² (bigger means more crowded) say the same fact in opposite directions. Looking at only the number of students or only the area, or subtracting two quantities with different units, cannot tell how crowded it is.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Doyun's solution.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write, with units, what each of the two values you calculated (1.5 and 1.33…) is the value of.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.hint.1: Explain in words which gives students more room, a classroom where one person uses a big area or one where one person uses a small area.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.line.0: Room 가: 36 ÷ 24 = 1.5, so it is 1.5 m² per student.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.line.1: Room 나: 40 ÷ 30 = 1.33…, so it is about 1.33 m² per student.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.line.2: 1.5 is greater than 1.33…, so Room 가 is more crowded.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the more crowded of the two rooms is Room 가.
y-m-17-06.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The bigger the area one student uses, the roomier it is, so it is less crowded. Room 가, with 1.5 m² per student, is less crowded than Room 나, with about 1.33 m², and the more crowded room is Room 나. Line 4 carried over the mistake of line 3.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.prompt: Make three different versions of Room 나 that is less crowded than Room 가. The number of students is from 20 to 40, the floor area is from 20 m² to 80 m², and all are natural numbers.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.hint.0: Decide the number of students, and think about how many m² the floor must be for that number of students to get 1.5 m² each. It must be bigger than that.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.hint.1: Find the area per person of the room you made, compare it with 1.5, and check that you did not go outside the ranges for the number of students and the floor.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.ok.c1: The number of students is a natural number from 20 to 40.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.fail.c1: The number of students is not a natural number from 20 to 40.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.ok.c2: The floor area is a natural number from 20 m² to 80 m².
y-m-17-06.s.s3.fail.c2: The floor area is not a natural number from 20 to 80.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.ok.c3: The area per person is bigger than in Room 가 (1.5 m²).
y-m-17-06.s.s3.fail.c3: The area per person is 1.5 m² or less, the same as Room 가. Think about which floor must be bigger when the number of students is the same.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.explain: e.g. (20 students, 31 m²) is 1.55 m² per person, (24 students, 40 m²) is about 1.67 m², (30 students, 50 m²) is about 1.67 m², and (40 students, 61 m²) is about 1.53 m², all bigger than 1.5 m². With 30 students, the floor must be bigger than 45 m². (30 students, 45 m²) is 1.5 m² per person, the same as Room 가, so it is not a less crowded room.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.prompt: Write, using numbers, how you compared one of the rooms you chose with Room 가.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.hint.0: Choose one of the rooms you made above and write its number of students and floor area as they are.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.hint.1: Find the area per person by the same standard as Room 가, compare which is bigger, and write it as a sentence.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.placeholder: e.g. Room 나 has ... students and a floor of ... m², so ...
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the area per person is greater than 1.5 m²?
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid judging by only one of the number of students and the floor area?
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether using another comparison method gives the same conclusion?
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.model.0: Room 나 has 30 students and a floor of 50 m², so per person it is 50÷30, about 1.67 m². Room 가 has 1.5 m² per person, so Room 나 gives each person a bigger area and is less crowded.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.model.1: I chose a room with 40 students and a floor of 61 m². Per 1 m² there are 40÷61, about 0.66 students, while Room 가 has 24÷36, about 0.67 students. Room 가 has more students per 1 m², so Room 나 is less crowded.
y-m-17-06.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: An answer that compared by students per 1 m².

y-m-17-07.title: Rewriting the school newspaper's ‘up 5%’
y-m-17-07.topic: Saying a change in percentage precisely
y-m-17-07.goal: Tell whether ‘up 5%’ is a change in the rate or a change in the number of people, and rewrite the sentence with numbers so readers don't misunderstand.
y-m-17-07.material: The school newspaper ran this article. “The students who come to school by bicycle rose 5%, from 25% two years ago to 30% this year.” The total number of students was 200 in both years (the total did not change). One reader read it as “Then that means 10 more students,” and another read it as “It says up 5%, so 50 students became about 52 or 53.”
y-m-17-07.thinking.0: Telling apart different meanings of the same number
y-m-17-07.thinking.1: Revising the wording with the reader in mind
y-m-17-07.thinking.2: Comparing rates that change with the base quantity
y-m-17-07.prereq.0: Meaning of a percentage and its base quantity
y-m-17-07.prereq.1: Using a percentage to find the number in a part of the whole
y-m-17-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the explanations that match the numbers in the article (200 students in all, 25% to 30%).
y-m-17-07.s.s1.hint.0: Find how many of the 200 students 25% and 30% each are, and write them in a table.
y-m-17-07.s.s1.hint.1: Read separately whether the sentence about ‘5%’ is about the total of 200 students or about the original number of bicycle riders.
y-m-17-07.s.s1.o.a: The students who come to school by bicycle went from 50 to 52 or 53
y-m-17-07.s.s1.r.a: You read it as 5% of 50 being the increase. Calculate how many students 30% actually is and compare.
y-m-17-07.s.s1.o.b: The total number of students grew, so the share of bicycle riders grew
y-m-17-07.s.s1.r.b: The data says the total number of students did not change.
y-m-17-07.s.s1.o.c: The students who come to school by bicycle increased by 20% of the original number
y-m-17-07.s.s1.r.c: You compared the increase in the number of people with the original number. You read it with the number of people as the base.
y-m-17-07.s.s1.o.d: The share of bicycle riders among all the students rose from 25% to 30%
y-m-17-07.s.s1.r.d: You read that the rate itself changed. It is a change with the total number of students as the base.
y-m-17-07.s.s1.explain: 25% is 50 of 200 students and 30% is 60 of 200 students. The rate rose 5 percentage points, from 25% to 30%, and the number of people went from 50 to 60, an increase of 10, that is, 20% of the original. The article's ‘up 5%’ can be read as meaning the rate went up, but some readers read it as the number of people going up 5%.
y-m-17-07.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the article's sentence so readers do not get confused. Keep the total of 200 students, and write it so that both how the rate changed and how the number of people changed show.
y-m-17-07.s.s2.hint.0: First write the number of people in the two years, and find how much it increased.
y-m-17-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write one sentence each, distinguishing whether the ‘5%’ is about all the students or about the number of bicycle riders.
y-m-17-07.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The students who come to school by bicycle ...
y-m-17-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the change in rate and the change in number of people separately?
y-m-17-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid leaving an expression like ‘up 5%’ where it is confusing what the 5% is of?
y-m-17-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Even if the numbers were changed, would the reader still read it with the same meaning?
y-m-17-07.s.s2.model.0: The students who come to school by bicycle rose by 10, from 50 (25%) to 60 (30%) of the 200 students. Their share of the whole rose 5 percentage points, and in number of students it rose 20% from the beginning.
y-m-17-07.s.s2.model.1: Of the 200 students, those who come by bicycle were 25% (50 students) and became 30% (60 students), 10 more.
y-m-17-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that removed the ambiguity with two percentages and the number of people.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.prompt: The next year, the rate is said to have risen from 30% to 35% (the total is still 200 students). In both years the rate rose 5 percentage points. But what about the increase in the number of people compared with the ‘original number’?
y-m-17-07.s.s3.hint.0: Find the number of people in each year and organize the increase in number of people in a table.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put the increase of 10 side by side with the ‘original number’ of each year and compare the sizes.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.o.a: The rate rose by the same amount, so the increase in the number of people is also the same 20%
y-m-17-07.s.s3.r.a: Compare the increase of 10 with the original number in each case, when it goes from 50 to 60 and when it goes from 60 to 70.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.o.b: The increase in the number of people is bigger than the 20% of the first year
y-m-17-07.s.s3.r.b: The original number changed from 50 to 60. Think about what happens when the same 10 is compared with a bigger number.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.o.c: We can't compare because we can't tell what the original number is
y-m-17-07.s.s3.r.c: The original number is 60, which can be found from the data.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.o.d: The same 10 more, but the original number is bigger, so it is less than 20%
y-m-17-07.s.s3.r.d: This is a reading that compared the same 10 with a bigger original number.
y-m-17-07.s.s3.explain: In the first year, it went from 50 to 60, an increase of 10, which is 1/5 (20%) of the original, and in the next year it went from 60 to 70, an increase of 10, which is 1/6 (about 16.7%) of the original. Even if the rate rises by the same amount, saying the increase in people as a percentage of the original number can give a different value.

y-m-17-08.title: The distance a wheel rolled: is it okay to approximate pi as 3?
y-m-17-08.goal: Use cases you make yourself to check how much the circumference changes with the approximation of pi (3, 3.14), and explain that whether it is okay to use an approximation depends on the accuracy needed and the number of times rolled.
y-m-17-08.material: You roll a wheel-shaped measuring tool with a diameter of d cm along the ground to measure distance. The wheel does not slip, and when it rolls one turn it moves as far as the wheel's circumference. Some people approximate pi as 3 and some calculate with 3.14. The wheel's diameter d is a natural number from 20 cm to 80 cm, and the number of turns rolled n is a natural number from 1 to 50.
y-m-17-08.thinking.0: Judging the conditions under which an approximation is fine
y-m-17-08.thinking.1: Making cases where the difference is large
y-m-17-08.thinking.2: Explaining the process by which error builds up
y-m-17-08.prereq.0: Meaning of pi and finding a circle's circumference from its diameter
y-m-17-08.s.s1.prompt: Is it okay to approximate pi as 3 when finding the distance a wheel rolled? Choose the most suitable thought.
y-m-17-08.s.s1.hint.0: Find the distance a wheel with a diameter of 50 cm rolls in one turn using pi as 3 and as 3.14, and compare the difference.
y-m-17-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the difference between the two values changes when the same wheel is rolled 10 turns.
y-m-17-08.s.s1.o.a: Pi is 3.14, so you must always calculate with 3.14
y-m-17-08.s.s1.r.a: 3.14 is also an approximation of pi. When using an approximation, first comes ‘how accurate it needs to be.’
y-m-17-08.s.s1.o.b: Pi is close to 3, so calculating with 3 is always enough
y-m-17-08.s.s1.r.b: A small difference when rolling the wheel just once can grow the more times you roll.
y-m-17-08.s.s1.o.c: Calculating with 3 is okay only for one turn, and from two turns on it isn't
y-m-17-08.s.s1.r.c: It is true that the difference builds up, but there is no boundary like ‘from two turns on, no.’ It depends on how accurate it needs to be.
y-m-17-08.s.s1.o.d: It depends on how much error is allowed and how many turns were rolled
y-m-17-08.s.s1.r.d: This is the thinking that you must consider the allowed error and the number of rolls together.
y-m-17-08.s.s1.explain: Even if the difference for one turn is small, if you roll the wheel many times the difference builds up and gets big. You must choose the approximation depending on whether you want a rough idea or need an exact measure.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.prompt: Make two different cases where the difference between the distance calculated with pi as 3 and the distance calculated with 3.14 is 100 cm (1 m) or more.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a diameter and find how many cm the difference between the two approximations is for one turn.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a number of turns at which the difference from each turn, gathered over that many turns, would pass 100 cm, check it, and try once more with a different diameter.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The diameter is a natural number from 20 cm to 80 cm.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The diameter must be a natural number from 20 cm to 80 cm.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of turns is a natural number from 1 to 50.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of turns rolled must be a natural number from 1 to 50.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The difference between the two values is 100 cm or more.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The difference between the two values does not reach 100 cm. Find how many cm the difference from one turn is, and think about how many turns you need to roll.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.explain: e.g. If a wheel with a 50 cm diameter rolls 15 turns, it is 2355 cm with 3.14 and 2250 cm with 3, a difference of 105 cm. If a wheel with an 80 cm diameter rolls 10 turns, the difference is 112 cm. The difference for one turn is diameter × 0.14 (cm), and this builds up as many times as the number of turns.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the cases you made and write how much the result differs from the value calculated with 3.14 when pi is approximated as 3. Write one time when that difference is a problem and one time when it is fine.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Take the diameter and number of turns you made above as they are and calculate with each of the two values of pi.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare the difference when the wheel is rolled just once with the difference when it is rolled many times, side by side.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. If a wheel with a diameter of ... cm rolls ... turns, ...
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In your numerical example, did you find the distance with both 3.14 and 3?
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the difference for one turn with the difference for many turns?
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you give examples of ‘work that needs to be accurate’ and ‘work where a rough idea is fine’?
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.model.0: If a wheel with a 50 cm diameter rolls 15 turns, it is 2355 cm with 3.14 and 2250 cm with 3, a difference of 105 cm. When measuring a rope length to make something, a 1 m error is big, but for one turn it is only about 7 cm, so for a rough look 3 is fine.
y-m-17-08.s.s2.because.model.1: The more you roll the wheel, the more the small difference of one turn builds up and grows. With an 80 cm wheel and 10 turns, the difference is as much as 112 cm. If you need an exact measure you should use 3.14, and if you only need a rough estimate, 3 is enough.

y-m-17-09.title: How many kinds of cans can you make from one sheet of paper?
y-m-17-09.topic: Net of a cylinder: a can made by rolling paper
y-m-17-09.goal: Confirm that different cylinder-shaped cans are made depending on which direction a rectangular sheet is rolled, and find both the diameter and the height to fix the error in a solution.
y-m-17-09.material: There is a rectangular sheet of paper that is 18.84 cm wide and 31.4 cm long. You want to roll this paper and join the two ends to make a cylinder-shaped can that is open at the top and bottom. Join the paper without overlapping, and do not think about the thickness of the seam. Use 3.14 for pi, and use the paper as the rectangle it is.
y-m-17-09.thinking.0: Finding several solutions from one piece of information
y-m-17-09.thinking.1: Finding the wrong line in a solution
y-m-17-09.thinking.2: Making without omission the cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-17-09.prereq.0: Knowing that in the net of a cylinder the side is a rectangle whose width equals the circumference of the base
y-m-17-09.prereq.1: Switching between diameter and circumference with pi as 3.14
y-m-17-09.s.s1.prompt: How many kinds of cans can be made with this one sheet of paper? Choose the most suitable thought.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine the rectangle rolled along its width and rolled along its length, and say which side forms the circle in each.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.hint.1: When you roll it and join it, think about whether the length of the joined side equals the circumference of the circle at the top of the can.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.o.a: Only one. Because the size of the paper is fixed
y-m-17-09.s.s1.r.a: The paper can be rolled along its width or along its length. First check whether the direction of rolling and joining has been fixed.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.o.b: Two. There are two directions in which the paper can be rolled
y-m-17-09.s.s1.r.b: You found that the side that becomes the circumference differs depending on the direction in which the paper is rolled and joined.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.o.c: Countless. Because you can choose the diameter freely
y-m-17-09.s.s1.r.c: The circumference is fixed by the length of a side of the paper. If you choose the diameter freely, the paper will be short or left over.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.o.d: It can't be made. Because the paper is not a square
y-m-17-09.s.s1.r.d: A can can also be made from a rectangular sheet. You just need to decide which side to use as the circumference.
y-m-17-09.s.s1.explain: The length of the side that joins when the paper is rolled becomes the circumference of the base. You can roll it with the 18.84 cm width as the circumference, or with the 31.4 cm length as the circumference. So two different cans are made.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.prompt: Jia explained the can made by rolling with the 18.84 cm side as the circumference like this. Choose the wrong line.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.hint.0: Mark which side of the paper was used as the circumference and which as the height, and check whether the same side was used twice.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether the two sides that are not joined become the top and bottom edges of the can when the paper is rolled.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.line.0: If the paper is rolled along its width, 18.84 cm becomes the circumference of the base.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.line.1: Circumference = diameter × 3.14, so the diameter is 18.84 ÷ 3.14 = 6 cm.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.line.2: In this case the height of the can is the other length of the paper, 18.84 cm.
y-m-17-09.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. Since the 18.84 cm side became the circumference of the base, the height of the can is the other length of the paper, 31.4 cm. The same length cannot be used for both the circumference and the height. The circumference in line 1 and the diameter of 6 cm in line 2 are right.
y-m-17-09.s.s3.prompt: Write both of the different diameters and heights of cans that can be made from this paper. (Diameter d cm, height h cm)
y-m-17-09.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one side to use as the circumference and find the diameter from that side's length. Think about what part of the can the remaining side becomes.
y-m-17-09.s.s3.hint.1: Choose the other side as the circumference and make another one the same way, and check that the two cans are different.
y-m-17-09.s.s3.fail.c1: The diameter and height must be greater than 0.
y-m-17-09.s.s3.ok.c2: One side of the paper becomes the circumference and the other side becomes the height.
y-m-17-09.s.s3.fail.c2: The diameter and height do not match a can made from this paper. Decide whether the side used as the circumference is 18.84 cm or 31.4 cm, and check that the other side is used as the height.
y-m-17-09.s.s3.explain: If you roll with 18.84 cm as the circumference, the diameter is 18.84 ÷ 3.14 = 6 cm and the height is 31.4 cm. If you roll with 31.4 cm as the circumference, the diameter is 31.4 ÷ 3.14 = 10 cm and the height is 18.84 cm. There are only these two.

y-m-17-10.title: I put in a stone and the water level went up
y-m-17-10.topic: Volume of a rectangular prism and an object under water
y-m-17-10.goal: Test, with new information, the idea of finding an object's volume from the change in water level in a rectangular-prism tank, and revise your judgment when the condition that the object is completely under water does not hold.
y-m-17-10.material: There is a tank shaped like a rectangular prism. Inside it is 30 cm wide, 20 cm long, and 20 cm tall, and it holds water up to a height of 10 cm. When a stone is put into the water, the water rises by as much as the stone pushes aside. The stone does not soak up water, and the thickness of the tank's walls is ignored.
y-m-17-10.thinking.0: Revising a prediction with new information
y-m-17-10.thinking.1: Finding the conditions under which the method for finding volume holds
y-m-17-10.prereq.0: How to find the volume of a rectangular prism
y-m-17-10.prereq.1: That the part holding water can also be seen as a rectangular prism
y-m-17-10.s.s1.prompt: Each time new information comes out, choose your thinking, and look at how your thinking changes before and after the information.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first find how many cm the water level rose and the volume of the part that rose.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether your thinking from the previous step fits the new information, and if some part does not fit, find what you had assumed.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.info: When one stone was put in so that it was completely under water, the water level became 12 cm. The water did not overflow.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: What would happen if all 6 identical stones were put in so that they are completely under water?
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.after: If one stone raised it 2 cm, 6 stones would try to raise it 12 cm to make 22 cm. The tank is 20 cm tall, so the water overflows. Whether the stones pile up and stick out of the water has to be checked separately.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The water will overflow. Because each stone raises the water level by 2 cm, so it would try to reach 22 cm
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You multiplied the height one stone raised up to 6 stones and compared it with the height of the tank.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The water will not overflow. Because it only rose to 12 cm, which is less than the tank height of 20 cm
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You judged the case of 6 stones from the result for one. Think about what happens as the number grows.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It isn't settled, because I don't know what happens if the stones overlap or pile up
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a careful thought that even considered the possibility of the stones piling up and sticking out of the water.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.info: When the same stones were put in one at a time, with 5 stones the water level was 20 cm and the tank was full, and when the sixth stone went in the water overflowed. All the stones were under water.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: What can you say from this result?
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.after: It rose 2 cm five times from 10 cm to reach 20 cm, so the rule fits. This rule can be used only while the stones are all under water and the water does not overflow.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The rule that one stone raises the level 2 cm fits this result
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You confirmed with the rule the result that it is full at 5 stones.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The more stones there are, the less each one raises the level
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Calculate whether this fits the result that it reached exactly 20 cm at 5 stones.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The rule is right, but it could change if the condition that the stones are all under water fails
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a thought that also looked at the condition under which the rule holds.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.info: This time a long stone 14 cm tall was put in standing on the bottom. When the water was 10 cm, the top of the stone stuck out of the water, and the water level became 11 cm.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can you say about this stone's volume?
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.after: If it is only partly under water, the volume of water pushed aside is the volume of the part under water (600 cm³). The volume of the whole stone is greater than 600 cm³, because the part above the water is added to the part under water.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The water level rose 1 cm, so it is 30 × 20 × 1 = 600 cm³
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You used the method of finding volume from the change in height just as it is. Check whether the stone was completely under water.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is greater than the 600 cm³ found from the change in water level. Because the part sticking out of the water did not push aside any water
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You even read that the part that was not under water was left out of the calculation.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is less than 600 cm³. Because it pushed aside less than the amount the water rose
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Compare again whether the volume of water pushed aside and the volume of the whole stone are the same.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.o.d: We can't tell. Because the stone's shape is not regular
y-m-17-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even if you don't know the exact value, you can say its minimum size.
y-m-17-10.s.s1.reflect: If you first chose ‘it overflows,’ write whether the second piece of information added confidence to that judgment; if you chose ‘if they pile up, I don't know,’ write which information relieved that worry. Also think about what the ‘method of finding’ was relying on in the third piece of information.
y-m-17-10.s.s2.prompt: A friend said, “If you multiply the difference in water level before and after putting in the stone by the width and length, you get the stone's volume.” Can this method always be used? Write when it can be used and when it can't.
y-m-17-10.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the value you calculated at the step where the stone was only partly under water (the third piece of information) with the volume of the whole stone.
y-m-17-10.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether, at the step where the water was full and overflowed (the second piece of information), you can find the volume by measuring the water level.
y-m-17-10.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. This method can be used when ... but when ... it ...
y-m-17-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you state, as a condition, whether the stone is completely under water?
y-m-17-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you think about why you can't know the volume from the difference in height when the water overflows?
y-m-17-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: When it can't be used, did you think about whether the real volume is bigger or smaller than the value found from the difference in height?
y-m-17-10.s.s2.model.0: It is right only when the stone is completely under water and the water does not overflow. If the stone is only partly under water, the water pushed aside is only as much as the part under water, so the value comes out smaller than the real volume.
y-m-17-10.s.s2.model.1: If the water overflows, you can't measure the height it rose, and if the stone sticks out of the water, that part does not go into the calculation. You should use it only when the stone is completely under water.
y-m-17-10.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that mentioned both overflowing and not being under water.

y-m-17-11.title: What solid shape has 24 edges?
y-m-17-11.topic: Parts of prisms and pyramids (edges, vertices, faces)
y-m-17-11.goal: Know that the number of edges alone does not fix one solid shape, find all the possible solids, and pick out the clue needed to fix just one.
y-m-17-11.material: A riddle card says, “I am a solid shape. I have 24 edges.” The solid shape is either a prism or a pyramid, and its base is a polygon with 3 or more sides. An edge is a line segment where one face meets another face.
y-m-17-11.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-17-11.thinking.1: Finding several cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-17-11.thinking.2: Choosing a clue that separates the cases
y-m-17-11.prereq.0: Edges, vertices, and faces of prisms and pyramids
y-m-17-11.prereq.1: The numbers of parts that change with the number of sides of the base
y-m-17-11.s.s1.prompt: Can this clue alone fix the solid shape as one?
y-m-17-11.s.s1.hint.0: Organize how the edges of a prism and of a pyramid are counted using the number of sides of the base.
y-m-17-11.s.s1.hint.1: Changing the number of sides of the base, find the cases where there are 24 edges, in prisms and in pyramids separately.
y-m-17-11.s.s1.o.a: Yes, it can be fixed. It is an octagonal prism
y-m-17-11.s.s1.r.a: You thought only of prisms and did not check whether a pyramid could also have 24 edges.
y-m-17-11.s.s1.o.b: Yes, it can be fixed. It is a dodecagonal pyramid
y-m-17-11.s.s1.r.b: You thought only of pyramids and did not check whether a prism could also have 24 edges.
y-m-17-11.s.s1.o.c: No, it can't be fixed. Both a prism and a pyramid can have 24 edges
y-m-17-11.s.s1.r.c: You considered both prisms and pyramids and judged that it is not fixed as one.
y-m-17-11.s.s1.o.d: No, it can't be fixed. The number of edges differs from solid to solid, so it can't be a clue
y-m-17-11.s.s1.r.d: The number of edges is fixed by the number of sides of the base. It can be a clue, but it is not enough by itself.
y-m-17-11.s.s1.explain: A prism whose base has 8 sides (an octagonal prism) has 24 edges, and a pyramid whose base has 12 sides (a dodecagonal pyramid) also has 24 edges. So this clue alone cannot fix it as one.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.prompt: Find all the solid shapes with 24 edges and write them as different answers. Write the number of sides of the base as n, and write the type t as 1 for a prism and 2 for a pyramid.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.hint.0: Write how to count the edges of a prism using the number of sides of the base, and find the number of sides that gives 24.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.hint.1: Count the edges of a pyramid the same way, find the number of sides that gives 24, and check that it is a different solid from the prism above.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.var.n: Number of sides of the base
y-m-17-11.s.s2.ok.c1: The base has a natural number of sides that is 3 or more.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.fail.c1: The base must be a polygon with 3 or more sides.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.ok.c2: The type is a prism (1) or a pyramid (2).
y-m-17-11.s.s2.fail.c2: The type must be written as 1 (prism) or 2 (pyramid).
y-m-17-11.s.s2.fail.c3: There are not 24 edges. Write the number of edges of the type you chose in terms of the number of sides of the base and check.
y-m-17-11.s.s2.explain: They are the octagonal prism with 8 base sides (8 edges on one base + 8 edges on the other base + 8 side edges = 24) and the dodecagonal pyramid with 12 base sides (12 base edges + 12 side edges = 24). Only these two.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.prompt: If you add just one more clue to this riddle, which ones would let you fix the solid shape as one? Choose all of them.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number of vertices, the number of faces, and the shape of the side faces of the two candidates in a table, and find where the two candidates are different.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.hint.1: For each choice, check whether the two candidates have the same value or a different value.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.r.a: This is the thinking of counting the vertices of each solid to check whether it can separate the two candidates.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.r.b: The height can be 5 cm in both candidates.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.r.c: Both candidates have a polygon as the base. It is a condition already given in the problem.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.o.d: All the side faces are triangles
y-m-17-11.s.s3.r.d: This is the thinking of checking whether the shape of the side faces differs between the two candidates.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.r.e: This is the thinking of counting the faces of each solid to check whether it can separate the two candidates.
y-m-17-11.s.s3.explain: The octagonal prism has 16 vertices and 10 faces, and its side faces are rectangles. The dodecagonal pyramid has 13 vertices and 13 faces, and its side faces are triangles. 16 vertices, all side faces being triangles, and 13 faces can separate the two, while the height or ‘the base is a polygon’ cannot.

y-m-17-12.title: The tank holds only 0.048 L of water?
y-m-17-12.topic: Changing units of volume: m³, cm³, L
y-m-17-12.goal: Find the mistake in a solution that used the relation between length units directly for volume units, choose a way to check whether the result makes sense, and rewrite it correctly.
y-m-17-12.material: There is a tank shaped like a rectangular prism. It is 1.2 m long, 0.8 m wide, and 0.5 m tall, and think of the inside as the same size. How many L of water does this tank hold when it is filled to the top? Subin solved it as below but felt the answer was strange.
y-m-17-12.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
y-m-17-12.thinking.1: Checking whether a result makes sense
y-m-17-12.prereq.0: How to find the volume of a rectangular prism
y-m-17-12.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Subin's solution.
y-m-17-12.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether changing a length of 1 m to 100 cm is right, and whether you can use 100 just the same when changing a volume of 1 m³.
y-m-17-12.s.s1.hint.1: Change a cube with 1 m sides to its side length in cm and find its volume directly.
y-m-17-12.s.s1.line.3: 1 L = 1000 cm³, so 48 cm³ = 0.048 L. This tank holds 0.048 L of water.
y-m-17-12.s.s1.explain: The mistake starts in line 2. 1 m is 100 cm, but a volume of 1 m³ is the volume of a cube with 1 m sides, so it is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1000000 cm³. Lines 3 and 4 carried over the wrong conversion and became wrong values. The calculation in line 1 is right.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.prompt: Which checks help you notice that Subin's result (0.048 L) is strange? Choose all the suitable ones.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.hint.0: Compare in words the size of the tank with the size of one milk carton (1 L).
y-m-17-12.s.s2.hint.1: Solve it in a different order from Subin (changing all the lengths to cm from the start) and check that the two results are the same.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.o.a: Press the same calculation on a calculator once more to see whether the same value comes out
y-m-17-12.s.s2.r.a: If you calculate with the same thinking, the same value comes out again. Whether the calculation is right and whether the conversion is right are different matters.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.o.b: Compare the size of the tank with the size of a 1 L milk carton
y-m-17-12.s.s2.r.b: You checked whether the result makes sense by comparing with the size of a real object.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.o.c: Erase the units and judge the size by the numbers alone
y-m-17-12.s.s2.r.c: When the unit changes, the same number is a completely different size. The heart of the problem is whether the unit is wrong.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.o.d: Change all the lengths to cm from the start, solve again, and compare
y-m-17-12.s.s2.r.d: You solved again in a different order and compared the results. It is a check of whether the value is the same regardless of the order of conversion.
y-m-17-12.s.s2.explain: If you remember that the tank is much bigger than a milk carton, or change to cm from the start and compare by calculating 120 × 80 × 50, you can tell that 0.048 L is strange. Repeating the same calculation or erasing the units does not reveal the mistake.
y-m-17-12.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite line 3 correctly, and find how many L of water this tank holds. Also write how you knew.
y-m-17-12.s.s3.hint.0: Since 1 m is 100 cm, change the side of a cube with 1 m sides into cm and find its volume.
y-m-17-12.s.s3.hint.1: Check that the method of changing all the lengths to cm first and multiplying also gives 480 L.
y-m-17-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you think of 1 m³ as a cube with 100 cm sides?
y-m-17-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart whether you multiplied after changing the units or changed the units after multiplying?
y-m-17-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether the 480 L you found is an amount that makes sense?
y-m-17-12.s.s3.model.0: 1 m³ is a cube with 100 cm sides, so it is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1000000 cm³. So 0.48 m³ is 480000 cm³, and 1000 cm³ is 1 L, so it is 480 L.
y-m-17-12.s.s3.model.1: You can also change to cm from the start and calculate 120 × 80 × 50 = 480000 cm³. Writing 1 m³ = 100 cm³ was the mistake of using the length 100 for volume as well. 480000 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 480 L.
y-m-17-12.s.s3.modelNote.1: The method of changing to cm from the start.
